arXiv:2206.03505v1 [quant-ph] 07 Jun 2022

Quantum Resources Required to Block-Encode a Matrix of Classical Data

B. David Clader Affiliation: Goldman Sachs & Co., New York, NY, USA Email: dave.clader@gs.com    Alexander M. Dalzell Affiliation: AWS Center for Quantum Computing, Pasadena, CA, USA Affiliation: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA    Nikitas Stamatopoulos Affiliation: Goldman Sachs & Co., New York, NY, USA    Grant Salton Affiliation: Amazon Quantum Solutions Lab, Seattle, WA, USA Affiliation: AWS Center for Quantum Computing, Pasadena, CA, USA Affiliation: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA    Mario Berta Affiliation: AWS Center for Quantum Computing, Pasadena, CA, USA Affiliation: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA Affiliation: Department of Computing, Imperial College London, London, UK    William J. Zeng Affiliation: Goldman Sachs & Co., New York, NY, USA
Abstract

We provide modular circuit-level implementations and resource estimates for several methods of block-encoding a dense N×NN\times N matrix of classical data to precision ϵ\epsilon; the minimal-depth method achieves a TT-depth of 𝒪⁡(log⁡(N/ϵ)),\mathcal{O}(\log(N/\epsilon)), while the minimal-count method achieves a TT-count of 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡(1/ϵ))\mathcal{O}(N\log(1/\epsilon)). We examine resource tradeoffs between the different approaches, and we explore implementations of two separate models of quantum random access memory (QRAM). As part of this analysis, we provide a novel state preparation routine with TT-depth 𝒪⁡(log⁡(N/ϵ))\mathcal{O}(\log(N/\epsilon)), improving on previous constructions with scaling 𝒪⁡(log2⁡(N/ϵ))\mathcal{O}(\log^{2}(N/\epsilon)). Our results go beyond simple query complexity and provide a clear picture into the resource costs when large amounts of classical data are assumed to be accessible to quantum algorithms.

I Introduction

I.1 Motivation

A commonly used access model for quantum algorithms requiring classical data is a so-called “block-encoding” of the classical data into a unitary operator. Costs associated with these algorithms are often quoted in terms of the asymptotic scaling of the number of queries to the block-encoding oracle. However, if we are to make assessments about the potential of QRAM (QRAM)-based algorithms, we must take into account the cost of each block-encoding query as well. In this work, we provide a detailed implementation and resource comparison of different methods one might use to block-encode a dense matrix AA representing classical data.

Block-encodings for N×NN\times N matrices11 1 Block-encodings for non-square matrices are a straightforward extension of the square case. We show how to do this in App. A.1. are useful because they can, in principle, be implemented in exponentially small time (i.e., with quantum circuits of depth only polylog​(N)\text{polylog}(N) Chakraborty et al. [2019]), albeit still with space cost of 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) qubits. The block-encoding framework has proven useful for quantum algorithms for a variety of applications. Together with insights from adiabatic quantum computing, block-encoding has been crucial to the discovery of quantum linear system solvers with provably optimal scaling with respect to relevant parameters Gilyén et al. [2019a], Subaşı et al. [2019], Costa et al. [2021], An and Lin [2022]. The framework has led to faster algorithms for phase estimation Rall [2021], quantum gradients Gilyén et al. [2019b], and improved Hamiltonian simulation and regression techniques Low and Chuang [2019], Chakraborty et al. [2019]. Furthermore, block-encoding has been used to analyze quantum optimization algorithms Kerenidis and Prakash [2020], Augustino et al. [2021] and related algorithms for portfolio optimization Kerenidis et al. [2019]. Many of these algorithms make use of the QSVT (QSVT) algorithm Gilyén et al. [2019a], Martyn et al. [2021], which uses a technique known as QSP (QSP) Low et al. [2016], Low and Chuang [2019] that performs polynomial transformations on the block-encoded matrix.

I.2 Model

A unitary matrix UAU_{A} block-encodes the matrix A∈ℝN×NA\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} when the top-left block of UAU_{A} is proportional to AA, i.e.

UA=(A/α⋅⋅⋅),U_{A}=\begin{pmatrix}A/\alpha&\cdot\\ \cdot&\cdot\end{pmatrix}, (1)

where α≥‖A‖\alpha\geq||A|| is a normalization constant. We use ||⋅||||\cdot|| to denote the operator norm. The other blocks in UAU_{A} are irrelevant, but they must be encoded such that UAU_{A} is unitary. Note that we focus on real matrices AA, but the extension to complex matrices is straightforward.

There is a variety of techniques available to block-encode a matrix Gilyén et al. [2019a], Chakraborty et al. [2019]. For applications where we wish to operate on dense, classical data, such as is often encountered in machine learning or finance applications, a particularly relevant method is the QRAM input model and its many proposed implementations Giovannetti et al. [2008a], Giovannetti et al. [2008b], Matteo et al. [2020], Paler et al. [2020], Hann et al. [2021]. More concretely, we refer to QRAM as the quantum circuit that allows query access to classical data in superposition

∑jαj​|j⟩​|0⟩​⟶QRAM​∑jαj​|j⟩​|bj⟩,\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}\ket{j}\ket{0}\overset{\text{QRAM}}{\longrightarrow}\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}\ket{j}\ket{b_{j}}, (2)

where jj is the address in superposition with amplitude αj\alpha_{j} and |bj⟩\ket{b_{j}} is the classical data loaded into a quantum state. In this work, we discuss two different circuit-level approaches to accomplish the QRAM operation, which are optimized for different objectives. The first is a select-swap (SS) model, which is particularly efficient in terms of TT-gate utilization Low et al. [2018]. The second is a bucket-brigade (BB) model Giovannetti et al. [2008a], which has reduced susceptibility to errors when operated on potentially faulty hardware Hann et al. [2021]. We also provide a variant of the select-swap QRAM approach that performs a slightly different version of Eq. (2), where a more general single-qubit state can be loaded controlled by a flag qubit.

The block-encoding constructions presented in our work compile all circuits into Clifford gates and TT gates, where attempts are made to minimize either the total number of qubits, the total number of TT gates—henceforth called the TT-count—or the minimum number of layers of parallel TT gates—henceforth called the TT-depth. Our estimates, as overviewed in the next subsection, illustrate the trade-offs between these three metrics. We focus on TT gates since, in many proposals for fault-tolerant quantum computation based on quantum error-correcting codes like the surface code, Clifford gates are transversal and can be performed essentially for free (or in some cases by simply updating the Pauli frame for the decoder completely in software). Meanwhile, TT gates require the expensive process of magic state distillation Knill [2004], Bravyi and Kitaev [2005]. Indeed, the motivating model for our work is one in which the logical quantum circuits we describe are carried out with lattice surgery Horsman et al. [2012], Litinski and Oppen [2018], Litinski [2019], Chamberland and Campbell [2022] on many physical qubits encoded with the surface code. We additionally assume that logical CNOT gates can be performed between arbitrary qubits in constant time, and that the fanout-CNOT operation, i.e. the product of many CNOTs with the same control but different targets, can be performed in constant time Litinski and Oppen [2018]. As such, our calculations can be seen as optimistic and could be underestimates if there are additional hardware-specific constraints on logical topology and connectivity.

I.3 Overview of results

The main contributions of our work are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Clifford+TT circuits with minimal TT-depth, or alternatively, with minimal TT-count, to perform a block-encoding unitary UAU_{A} as given in Eq. (1) for N×NN\times N matrices AA

  • •

    Resource calculations for the block-encoding, including all constant factors, expressed in terms of a small number of tunable parameters

  • •

    Clifford+TT circuits for QRAM and state preparation sub-routines, along with associated resource calculations

  • •

    Conceptual improvements to state preparation procedure yielding quadratic speedup in TT-depth complexity.

Our results for the circuit resource costs in terms of the number of qubits, TT-count, and TT-depth are shown in the top part of Tab. 1, including constant factors. We note that the cost of a having the TT-depth be exponentially smaller than the time needed even to write down all of the matrix entries is a large overhead of 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) ancilla qubits and total TT-count. It is possible to reduce the qubit and TT-count to 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) at the cost of making TT-depth grow also to 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N).

In addition to parameterized resource estimates, we compute the exact costs to block-encode matrices of sizes [16×16,256×256,4096×4096][16\times 16,256\times 256,4096\times 4096] with precision ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01. To estimate a matrix norm, needed for the scale factor α\alpha, we took the entries to be uniformly distributed random numbers on the interval [5.0,105.0][5.0,105.0] as representative of the type of data we might choose to block-encode (e.g., financial market data). Example numbers are shown in the bottom part of Tab. 1.

I.4 Block-encoding strategy

In order to make the definition from Eq. (1) precise, we provide quantum circuits that perform a unitary U~A\tilde{U}_{A} on n+ℓn+\ell qubits, where N=2nN=2^{n} for which

‖A−α⁡(⟨0|ℓ⊗I)​U~A​(|0⟩ℓ⊗I)‖=α⁡‖(⟨0|ℓ⊗I)​(UA−U~A)​(|0⟩ℓ⊗I)‖≤ϵ,\left\lVert A-\alpha(\bra{0}_{\ell}\otimes I)\tilde{U}_{A}(\ket{0}_{\ell}\otimes I)\right\rVert=\alpha\left\lVert(\bra{0}_{\ell}\otimes I)(U_{A}-\tilde{U}_{A})(\ket{0}_{\ell}\otimes I)\right\rVert\leq\epsilon, (3)

where the parameter ℓ\ell denotes the number of ancillas, II denotes the identity on nn qubits, and ∥⋅∥\lVert\cdot\rVert denotes the operator norm.22 2 If NN is not a power of 2, we can pad the matrix with zeros such that this is the case. Subscripts on bras and kets are included for clarity to indicate the associated number of qubits in the state. Following standard convention, we call U~A\tilde{U}_{A} a (α,ℓ,ϵ)(\alpha,\ell,\epsilon)-block-encoding of AA. The normalization factor for the block-encoding we treat is α=‖A‖F\alpha=||A||_{F}, where ||⋅||F||\cdot||_{F} denotes the Frobenius norm.33 3 One can use a different norm (the q-norm), which we discuss in App. A.2.

All of our constructions follow the prescription laid out in Refs. Kerenidis and Prakash [2016], Gilyén et al. [2019a], Chakrabarti et al. [2020], which calls for forming UAU_{A} as the product of a pair of controlled-state preparation unitaries ULU_{L} and URU_{R}. In this prescription,

UA=UR†​UL,U_{A}=U_{R}^{\dagger}U_{L}\,, (4)

where, controlled on an nn-qubit register in the state |j⟩n\ket{j}_{n}, URU_{R} prepares the nn-qubit state |ψj⟩n\ket{\psi_{j}}_{n}, and ULU_{L} prepares the state |ϕj⟩n\ket{\phi_{j}}_{n} with the assistance of ℓ′\ell^{\prime} QRAM ancilla qubits44 4 The unitary ULU_{L} additionally swaps the two nn-qubit registers, cf. Fig. I.4.. That is, we have

UR​|0⟩n​|0⟩ℓ′​|j⟩n=|ψj⟩n​|0⟩ℓ′​|j⟩nandUL​|0⟩n​|0⟩ℓ′​|k⟩n=|k⟩n​|0⟩ℓ′​|ϕk⟩n.\displaystyle U_{R}\ket{0}_{n}\ket{0}_{\ell^{\prime}}\ket{j}_{n}=\ket{\psi_{j}}_{n}\ket{0}_{\ell^{\prime}}\ket{j}_{n}\quad\text{and}\quad U_{L}\ket{0}_{n}\ket{0}_{\ell^{\prime}}\ket{k}_{n}=\ket{k}_{n}\ket{0}_{\ell^{\prime}}\ket{\phi_{k}}_{n}\,. (5)

We then choose

|ψj⟩n=∑k=0N−1Aj​k‖Aj,⋅‖​|k⟩nand|ϕk⟩n=∑j=0N−1‖Aj,⋅‖‖A‖F​|j⟩n(independent of k),\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{j}}_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{A_{jk}}{||A_{j,\cdot}||}\ket{k}_{n}\quad\text{and}\quad\ket{\phi_{k}}_{n}=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\frac{||A_{j,\cdot}||}{||A||_{F}}\ket{j}_{n}\quad\text{(independent of $k$),} (6)

where Aj,⋅A_{j,\cdot} denotes the jj-th row of AA and ‖Aj,⋅‖\|A_{j,\cdot}\| the standard Euclidean norm of that vector. Since |ϕk⟩n\ket{\phi_{k}}_{n} is independent of kk, ULU_{L} is simply state preparation, rather than controlled-state preparation. However, in the q-norm version of the block-encoding presented in App. A.2, |ϕk⟩n\ket{\phi_{k}}_{n} will depend on kk. It is easily verified that UAU_{A} is an exact block-encoding of AA, i.e.,

(⟨0|ℓ⊗⟨j|n)​UA​(|0⟩ℓ⊗|k⟩n)=Aj​kwith ℓ=n+ℓ′.(\bra{0}_{\ell}\otimes\bra{j}_{n})U_{A}(\ket{0}_{\ell}\otimes\ket{k}_{n})=A_{jk}\quad\text{with $\ell=n+\ell^{\prime}$.} (7)

We refer to Fig. I.4 for an overview of this reduction from block-encoding to controlled-state preparation. To implement the controlled-state preparation unitaries URU_{R} and ULU_{L}, we combine a QRAM-like data-loading step with a protocol for state preparation of nn-qubit states.
